summary:
Earth Trend Detective is a free web map that shows how the land in 170 countries changed from 2002 to 2025. It runs on NASA’s GLDAS Noah V2.1 land model and follows five things: air temperature, how wet the land is, rain, water draining below the soil, and how much water plants use.

For every place we fit a trend line and test it (Sen’s slope, Mann-Kendall with pre-whitening, false-discovery control). A country gets colour only when its change passes those tests. Everywhere else the map says “no clear trend yet”, so a few unusual years can’t pass for a climate signal. Before opening the newer data, we wrote down 82 predictions from older NASA data. 60 came true.

Click a country and you get the yearly chart, what the change means for farmers, water managers, health and business, and 13 sourced examples of what other countries did about the same problem. The site works in English and Arabic; the Arabic place summaries were written by Fanar, Qatar’s Arabic AI model, and checked against our numbers.

We built it in Doha with Qatar in mind: around 80% of the calories Qatar eats are imported, so the climate on its suppliers’ farms matters as much as the weather at home.
details:
Earth Trend Detective is a web map of how the land changed in 170 countries from 2002 to 2025. You type a city or a country, and a card opens with five measures: air temperature, how wet the land surface is, rain, water draining below the soil, and how much water plants use. Each one gets a verdict (hotter or cooler, wetter or drier, more or less), the size of the change, a yearly chart, and a certainty level: Clear, Early sign, or No clear trend yet.

How it works. We downloaded the NASA GLDAS Noah Land Surface Model V2.1 monthly data (GES DISC) for the whole globe, took a 1.25° lattice of 9,715 land cells and turned it into calendar-year means. For every cell and every country we estimate the change with Sen’s slope and test it with Mann-Kendall, plus a pre-whitened Mann-Kendall to catch runs of similar years. Benjamini-Hochberg controls false discoveries inside each measure and Benjamini-Yekutieli across all tests. A place is coloured only if it passes. Our pre-whitening code matches the pymannkendall library, and on a synthetic pure-noise world the pipeline colours zero cells.

We also tested ourselves before trusting the map. Using the older GLDAS V2.0 data we wrote down 82 trend predictions and locked the file, then opened V2.1: 60 of 82 held (binomial p ≈ 1.6e-5). On 2015-2025 alone, which the predictions never saw, 49 of 82 held. That is weaker, and we say so on the site.

Benefits and impact. Farmers, water managers, health workers and small businesses get the result in plain words, with what it means for them and 13 sourced examples of what other places did (Ahmedabad’s heat plan, Jordan’s As-Samra wastewater reuse, Abu Dhabi’s underground water bank and others). For Qatar, which imports around 80% of its calories, the same map is a quick climate check of supplier countries. The whole site switches to Arabic with right-to-left layout. The Arabic place summaries are written by Fanar, the Arabic language model from QCRI in Qatar, and our script checks every summary against our numbers before it is shown; 112 of 170 passed, the rest use a fixed Arabic template.

Tools. Python (NumPy, netCDF4, Shapely) for download and analysis, JavaScript with d3.js and TopoJSON for the map, Natural Earth for borders and cities, Playwright for browser tests, the Fanar API for Arabic, and Claude (Anthropic) as a coding and writing assistant. No special hardware: the global download ran on a laptop. The site is one self-contained HTML file that works offline.

What we considered. GLDAS is a model, not a measurement, and it has no groundwater pumping, so the site says this next to the numbers. We did not splice GLDAS 2.0 and 2.1, because in 2002-2014 the two versions differ by more than one standard deviation in most regions. Rain swings too much for 24 years to show a trend in most places, so for rain the map shows how unreliable it is instead of inventing a direction. Every reference was checked by hand, and claims we could not source were removed.
